sections.title: How Kudzu plays differently
sections.intro: The rules that differ from the FireRed you remember. The battle engine is Gen 9 (Scarlet/Violet) apart from what is listed here.

entries.text: A hard cap that rises as you go: a Pokémon at the cap gains no EXP at all, and Rare Candy can't take it past the cap. The current cap is in the top bar.
Pokémon never gain EVs, from battles or anything else. Stats come from level, base stats, IVs and nature only.

An item only goes away if it was actually used up in battle - a Berry eaten, a Focus Sash triggered, an item thrown with Fling, an Air Balloon popped. Anything merely taken away comes back after the battle: Knock Off, Trick and Switcheroo, Pickpocket and Magician, Corrosive Gas, Incinerate. Thief and Covet are plain attacks here and steal nothing.

entries.term: Tera Blast is a better Hidden Power
entries.text: 80 power, and its type comes from the user's IVs by the Hidden Power formula (a Pokémon with perfect IVs gets Dark). It is special, but becomes physical when the user's Attack is higher than its Sp. Atk.
They halve the target's Defense for the hit, as in Gen 3-4, which makes them hit twice as hard as in modern games.
Weather set by an ability (Drizzle, Drought, Sand Stream, Snow Warning) lasts the whole battle rather than five turns.
The opponent can put more than one of your Pokémon to sleep.

Some trainers start the battle with a field effect already up - a terrain, Trick Room, hazards on your side, or one of Kudzu's own: Magnetic Field, Twisted Vines, Riptide and Haunted Spirits. The trainer's page says which and what it does; they are all listed under Field effects below.
Two trainers who both spot you from the same tile fight you together in one double battle, and a few story fights are tag battles with an ally. The Trainers list shows each such pair as one entry.
The opponent's health box shows its HP as a percentage. In double battles, Start switches the opponents' boxes between the bar and the number.

sections.title: How the AI plays
sections.intro: Every trainer runs the same AI (Smart Trainer), modelled on Pokémon Run & Bun and Pokémon Null. Knowing how it decides makes most fights predictable - the Calc tab scores every opposing move for you and shows who comes in next.

entries.text: The AI sees your whole party: species, moves, abilities, held items and exact stats. It does not have to guess.

Every turn each of its moves starts at the same score and gains or loses points by rules; the highest score is used, and a tie is broken at random. Moves that would fail or do nothing are scored down and effectively never chosen.

It rolls damage for each of its attacks - a random roll between 85% and 100%, fresh every turn - and gives the one that rolled highest a bonus (+6, or +8 a quarter of the time). Any attack that would knock you out counts as the highest. So when two attacks are close, which one it picks changes from turn to turn.

Status moves have their own rules, and most of them reach the same +6 as the best attack when they are useful - so a Pokémon with a good status move and a good attack can go either way. Setup moves are judged by whether it can safely set up against what you have out.
It goes for the kill: an attack that knocks out your Pokémon always counts as its best attack. It also assumes a critical hit when its crit rate is at stage 3 or higher.

entries.term: Who comes in after a KO
entries.text: It checks every Pokémon left in its party against yours, in this order of preference: one that can trap yours; one that outspeeds and knocks yours out and wins the one-on-one; one that knocks yours out but is slower; one that 2-hits yours (faster first, then slower); one that resists your best attack and hits yours super-effectively; one that only resists; one that gains from healing waiting for it; a Baton Pass user; any that wins the one-on-one; and finally the one that does the most damage without being knocked out in one hit. When several Pokémon fit the matchup rules or the damage rule it takes the best of them; for the other rules it takes the one furthest down its party. A Pokémon switched in after a KO gets a free turn, so "wins the one-on-one" counts that.

Mid-battle it switches out when staying in is bad: all its moves are useless against yours, it is walled, badly statused, locked into a bad Choice move or an Encore, its attacking stats have been dropped, or it has a Pokémon that is immune to or absorbs the move you are likely to use. It won't switch into entry hazards that would knock the incoming Pokémon out.
Trainers that can Terastallize choose when it is worth it instead of doing it as soon as they can.
The first Pokémon in its party leads - except for the few trainers whose party order is shuffled every battle (RANDOMIZE_PARTY_INDICES under AI on the trainer's page).
It keeps track of you switching in a Pokémon that is immune to the move it chose, and stops falling for it.
In doubles the scoring is the same, and it avoids hitting its own partner with spread moves. The Calc tab's AI preview scores doubles as if they were singles, so treat its numbers as a guide there.
One stretch of the run, from one badge to the next. Each split has its locations in the order you reach them, its boss fights and its level cap.
Your one catch per area, the Nuzlocke rule. An area is one route, floor or fishing spot; the save file fills most of them in by itself from where each Pokémon was met.
Where fainted Pokémon go - boxes 13 and 14 in the game. The living PC is boxes 1 to 3.
How many opposing Pokémon each of yours has knocked out, read straight from the save.
A run of trainers back to back. The Multi Menu is switched off when you enter, so there is no healing and no box until the far end.
A trainer who stands between you and a mega stone: beating them gives it, or they watch or stand beside the spot where it lies.
What you spend on Hyper Training; the Bottle Caps page tracks how many the run has found and used.
